newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam steps up crackdown on corruption.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam steps up crackdown on corruption.

text.p: Communist Vietnam, stepping up its battle against the growing scourge of corruption, said on Monday that it would consider a new anti-graft bill that prescribes the death penalty for officials who rake off state funds.

A senior officer of the State Inspectorate said the draft bill suggested that any state or military official found guilty of siphoning off 300 million dong ($27,000) or more should go in front of the firing squad or at least be imprisoned for life.

"Work on fighting against corruption has not satisfied the people in the past," the official, who declined to be named, told Reuters. "So the party and the state still consider this as one of the four dangers."
"Some cases have been uncovered, but not dealt with strictly," he said. "In general, the crackdown on corruption has been insufficient."

The new bill would be the country's first legal document aimed at curbing graft, which has been fed in recent years by an environment of reform-led prosperity growth and continued state control in most sectors of the economy.
Earlier this year, a Hong Kong-based consultancy survey named China, Indonesia and Vietnam as Asia's most graft-ridden nations.
The official Hanoi Moi daily said on Monday that 4,900 corruption cases causing economic losses of over $145 million were uncovered in the first nine months of this year alone.

Corruption was one of the top issues at a Communist Party conference in June and several top leaders, including Prime Minister Vo Van Kiet and party leader Do Muoi, have since called for a new drive to root it out.
The state-controlled press has joined the call for a blitz on graft, giving intricate and murky details of several serious cases involving high-ranking officials.
Perhaps the most high-profile of those is the scandal surrounding Tamexco, a party-affiliated import-export company, via which some $50 million is said to have been embezzled.
State prosecuters said last week that 20 people, including three former top officials of the country's largest state-owned bank, would face trial for alleged involvement in the fraud case.
In another case, at least two senior anti-drug squad police officers have been arrested on suspicion of involvement in heroin trafficking.
On Monday, the Lao Dong newspaper also raised the question of a Hanoi People's Court judge who is alleged to have taken a bribe from a defendant in gold and cash.
Under the draft bill's proposals, state officials and army officers would be banned from setting up or managing a non-state business and receiving or offering gifts bought with state funds.
They would also be barred from depositing cash, gold or gems at foreign banks, a practice that allows bribes to be laundered, and from appointing relatives to positions such as accountant or cashier.
The State Inspectorate official said the death penalty threshold of $27,000 was, at this stage, only a suggestion.

According to official media reports, 104 people were sentenced to death in 1995. The human rights group Amnesty International has expressed concern about the growing use of the death penalty in Vietnam for cases involving economic crime.
